hero.headline.text: When the action is written in text,

hero.highlight.text: someone has to stop the model and parse it.

hero.takeaway.text: A text protocol relies on stop and a parser to turn the words the model wrote into an action; native tool calling hands that step to the provider. Remove stop, and the model may even make up the tool result for you.

concepts.01-text.description.text: Text action protocol: the model writes its thinking, the tool name, and the arguments after Thought, Action, and Action Input, and the program pulls the action out of the text with a regular expression.

concepts.02-stop.description.text: The program pastes the tool result back as an observation. The request carries stop: ["Observation:"], so the model is cut off when it writes this string, and control returns to the program.

concepts.03-fake.description.text: Without stop, the model may keep going and write an Observation and a final answer. Those numbers are guesses.

concepts.04-native.description.text: Native tool calling, also called function calling, puts the action in the response's tool_calls field. The provider parses it into structured fields, so the program doesn't have to parse free text.

section-1.paragraphs.0.text: A model's output is just text. To make it "do something", the program first has to read from the text what it wants to do. In {{lesson:tool-selection}}, the provider did this step: the model proposed a tool call in the tool_calls field, and after the runner executed it, the tool result went into a tool message. Early APIs had no such field, so every step of the model had to be written in plain text and understood by the program itself. Agreeing on a format in advance and then having the program parse it is called a text action protocol.

section-1.paragraphs.1.text: The most common format comes from the ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) pattern: the model alternately writes reasoning and an action, the program executes the action and hands back an observation, and the model decides the next step. Written as text, it is three lines: Thought followed by the thinking, Action followed by the tool name, and Action Input followed by the JSON arguments; when it can answer, it writes Final Answer instead. The program pastes the real result back as an Observation line, and the model carries on in the next round.

section-1.paragraphs.2.text: It is like filling in a form with a fixed layout rather than writing a letter: only if the layout is right can the program find "what to do" and "what the arguments are". Native tool calling can also implement ReAct; it just puts the action into a structured field. Learning the text format has two uses. Many frameworks, open-source projects, and local models that don't support native tool calling still use it. It also puts the division of labor, where the model proposes an action and the program executes it, out in the open. This lesson compares the two on the same question: look up the score of student s-1042's latest quiz and decide whether it is a pass.

predict-fabricated.prompt.text: Before you run "Without stop: s-1042", guess: will the model keep going after Action Input and write the Observation for the program? How many lesson.fabricated_observation events will this run produce (one for each Observation the model wrote itself)?

mq-who-executes.who-executes.prompt.text: In a text protocol, who executes the tool named in Action?

mq-who-executes.who-executes.a.text.text: The program: after parsing out the tool name and arguments, it calls the registered function

mq-who-executes.who-executes.a.feedback.text: Correct. The model only produces text; execution is always on the program's side.

mq-who-executes.who-executes.b.text.text: The model: writing an Action is the same as executing it

mq-who-executes.who-executes.b.feedback.text: Not quite. The model's output is only text, and nothing has been executed.

mq-who-executes.who-executes.c.text.text: The provider: it executes automatically once it recognizes an Action

mq-who-executes.who-executes.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The provider doesn't know this format; it just returned some text.

mq-who-executes.who-executes.explanation.text: The one who proposes the action and the one who executes it are separate, and that is true of native calling too.

section-2.title.text: stop: make the model stop where it should

section-2.paragraphs.0.text: In a text protocol, getting the model to stop after the action relies on the stop sequence in the request. The model should stop after writing Action Input and wait for the program to paste the real result back. But the model doesn't know "it's the program's turn now"; it just writes one token after another. This lesson's system prompt mentions Observation, and in the common ReAct demonstrations the line after Action Input is Observation. Following the format, the most natural thing to do is to write this line out too.

section-2.paragraphs.1.text: With the request parameter stop set to ["Observation:"], the provider cuts the output off when the model emits this string, and the returned content ends before it, usually without the string itself. The response's finish_reason is then usually stop. The cut is made by the provider and doesn't depend on the model's self-discipline, so it is more reliable than writing "stop when you're done" in the prompt. Whether stop is supported and how many stop sequences you can give differ by provider; follow the provider's documentation.

section-2.paragraphs.2.text: In the arm with stop, every request carries this parameter. Response 1 stops after Action Input. The program executes lookup_quiz_score, writes the result as "Observation: …", appends it as a user message, and sends request 2. After seeing the real score, the model writes Final Answer. stop has limits too: it matches only that exact string. If the model writes a variant, such as a lowercase "observation:" or "Observation :" with a space, stop doesn't catch it. This lesson's parser also splits only on Observation:, so such text stays as is in the assistant message put back into the context.

section-3.title.text: Without stop: the model writes the Observation for you

section-3.paragraphs.0.text: Remove stop, and the model may keep writing and produce even the tool result and the final answer for you. After Action Input it goes on to write "Observation: {"score": …}", then Final Answer. Those numbers are the model's guesses; it never saw the score table. If the program simply takes this Final Answer, the user gets a made-up score.

section-3.paragraphs.1.text: This lesson deliberately makes the score table irregular: s-1042 scored 73 on 4 attempts, s-2077 scored 58 on 2 attempts, and the passing line is 60. A made-up number shows up as soon as you compare it with the real result. The exercise "Without stop, a failing student" looks up s-2077: if the model guesses 80, its conclusion says the student passed, the exact opposite of the facts. A number that is slightly off may go unnoticed; a reversed conclusion misleads.

section-3.paragraphs.2.text: When the runner sees that the model wrote an Observation itself, it still executes the tool as usual, cuts out the self-written part and records it as a lesson.fabricated_observation event, and puts only the text before the Observation and the real result back into the context. The event lays out side by side what the model made up, the real result, and the Final Answer the model wrote from it, so you can compare them directly. Whether the model makes things up, and what it makes up, depends on the model you use, and the same model can differ from run to run; this run's record is what counts.

deep-dive-why-fabricate.title.text: Why the model writes the Observation for the program

deep-dive-why-fabricate.summary.text: The model continues the whole format, and it can't tell which line someone else is supposed to write.

deep-dive-why-fabricate.paragraphs.0.text: The model does just one thing: given the text so far, it writes the next token. This lesson's system prompt sets out the order: Thought, Action, Action Input, then wait for the Observation, then write Final Answer. ReAct examples in tutorials such as Hugging Face's also string these lines together into one complete record. When the JSON of Action Input ends, the most likely next line is "Observation:", and after that, the most likely thing is a piece of JSON that looks like a query result.

deep-dive-why-fabricate.paragraphs.1.text: The model isn't "lying". It doesn't know this line should wait for someone else to write it, and it has no way to actually look up the score table; the numbers it writes are just numbers that look plausible in that position. Unit 1 of the Hugging Face Agents Course demonstrates the same thing: asked about the weather in London without stop, the model wrote the Observation and the final answer in one go, with a temperature it made up; with stop added, the output ended after the action.

deep-dive-why-fabricate.paragraphs.2.text: Why doesn't native tool calling have this problem? A model trained for tool calling ends its output for that round after proposing a call, and the provider returns the call in tool_calls. In the next round's input, the tool result sits in a separate tool message supplied by the program. The model's output for this round has no slot left for a result.

mq-fabricated.fabricated-score.prompt.text: Without stop, the model wrote "Observation: {"score": 88}" after Action Input. In the score table, s-1042 has 73. What should the program do?

mq-fabricated.fabricated-score.a.text.text: Discard the Observation the model wrote, execute the tool, and continue with the real 73

mq-fabricated.fabricated-score.a.feedbac.text: Correct. An observation can only come from real execution.

mq-fabricated.fabricated-score.b.text.text: Use 88, since the model already gave a result

mq-fabricated.fabricated-score.b.feedbac.text: Not quite. The model never saw the score table; 88 is its guess.

mq-fabricated.fabricated-score.c.feedbac.text: Not quite. Made-up data must not take part in any calculation.

mq-fabricated.fabricated-score.explanati.text: The model can propose an action, but it can't supply the tool's result.

section-4.title.text: Record parse failures; don't quietly fix them

section-4.paragraphs.0.text: When the parser meets output that doesn't follow the format, it should record a failure and stop, not guess. Format is the other weakness of a text protocol: the model may leave out Action Input, may write the JSON as {student_id: s-1042} (neither key nor value quoted), or may just answer in a sentence with neither Action nor Final Answer.

section-4.paragraphs.1.text: The easiest thing is to guess: add the quotes, add the braces, dig the student ID out of the sentence. If the guess is right, you can't see that the model actually got it wrong, so there is no way to count how unstable the format is. If the guess is wrong, what gets executed is arguments the program made up, not the arguments the model proposed. Either way, the error becomes invisible.

section-4.paragraphs.2.text: This lesson's parser is lenient in only one way: it uses json.JSONDecoder.raw_decode from the Python standard library to read the JSON value at the start of Action Input, allowing a newline or other text to follow it. For example, if the arguments are followed by "let me look it up", the arguments can still be read. ["s-1042"] is valid JSON but not an object, so it still counts as a failure. Beyond that, any output that doesn't follow the format is recorded as a lesson.parse event with ok set to false, with the original text and the reason for the error, and the run stops.

section-4.paragraphs.3.text: There is one more case: the same output contains both an Action and a Final Answer. The parser executes the action first and does not adopt the conclusion, because the model wrote it before seeing the tool result. Every output leaves one lesson.parse, whether it succeeded or failed, containing the original text, the parse result, finish_reason, and model_wrote_observation, which says whether the model wrote an Observation itself this time.

deep-dive-format-errors.title.text: How other projects handle format errors

deep-dive-format-errors.summary.text: Hand the error back to the model to rewrite, or stop at once: what each approach values.

deep-dive-format-errors.paragraphs.0.text: Mini-SWE-Agent is an open-source agent for fixing code. Its text mode requires every model reply to contain exactly one command block fenced with three backticks, which it finds with a regular expression. Finding zero or more than one counts as a format error: the program hands the error message, together with a correct example, back to the model as a user message and asks it to rewrite; it stops only after consecutive errors reach a limit (3 by default). It also distinguishes one case: if finish_reason shows that the output was cut off by the length limit, the prompt says the answer was too long and truncated, rather than vaguely saying the format was wrong.

deep-dive-format-errors.paragraphs.1.text: This differs from the choice in this lesson, but doesn't contradict it. Handing the error back for a rewrite lets the run continue, which suits an agent that does real work; the price is that format problems get buried in the retry count and show up only if you count them specially. This lesson wants failures to stay visible as they are, so it stops at the first one. The approach of handing the error back to the model to rewrite was already shown in the limited repair of {{lesson:structured-output}}.

deep-dive-format-errors.paragraphs.2.text: Text mode is what Mini-SWE-Agent 1.0 and the earlier SWE-agent used. A comment in the 2.0 source says it strongly recommends switching to tool calling. The comment doesn't spell out the reason, but the retry mechanism above shows the cost: the format depends on the model getting it right every time, and every miss costs one more model call.

mq-parse.parse-trailing-text.prompt.text: The model wrote Action Input: {"student_id": "s-1042"} let me look it up. What does this lesson's parser do?

mq-parse.parse-trailing-text.a.text.text: It reads the student ID s-1042 from the arguments and hands it to the program to run the tool

mq-parse.parse-trailing-text.a.feedback.text: Correct. raw_decode reads only the one JSON value at the start, and the extra text after it doesn't matter.

mq-parse.parse-trailing-text.b.text.text: It records a parse failure, because there is text after the JSON

mq-parse.parse-trailing-text.b.feedback.text: Not quite. Allowing other text after the JSON is the parser's one leniency.

mq-parse.parse-trailing-text.c.text.text: It passes the whole line of text to the tool as the arguments

mq-parse.parse-trailing-text.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The arguments must be a parsed JSON object; the parser never hands the raw text to the tool.

mq-parse.parse-trailing-text.explanation.text: Leniency goes no further than reading the first JSON value; anything that isn't an object or isn't valid JSON is recorded as a parse failure.

section-5.title.text: Native tool calling hands parsing to the provider

section-5.paragraphs.0.text: Native tool calling hands the step of "finding the action in the text" to the provider, so the program gets ready-made fields. The native arm uses the same question but provides tools in the request, and the model returns the call in the tool_calls field. The tool name is a field value and the arguments are a JSON string, so there's nothing to find in free text. The finish_reason of this round is usually tool_calls, the program matches the result back by tool_call_id, and the result comes back in a message with role tool.

section-5.paragraphs.1.text: Native calls can go wrong too: the arguments may not be valid JSON, and the tool name may not be on the allowlist, as {{lesson:fail-safely}} already showed. The difference is that the error is in a structured field, so the program can locate it at a glance without guessing from a paragraph. Native calling also has no problem of fabricated observations: the model's output for this round ends at the call, and the tool result can only be brought back by the program in a tool message.

section-5.paragraphs.2.text: Compare the messages of request 2 and the difference is clear. The text protocol has four: system, user, an assistant holding the text before the Observation, and a last user message beginning with "Observation:" that carries the real result and looks like something the user said. Native calling also has four: system, user, an assistant with tool_calls, and a last message with role tool, which uses tool_call_id to say which call it answers. The tool result has its own message role and no longer has to pass as the user's words.

section-5.paragraphs.3.text: The division of labor in the two protocols is actually the same: the model proposes the action, the program executes it, and the real result is handed back. What changes is where the action is written, who reads it out, and what kind of message carries the result back. The experiment "Text protocol vs. native tool calling" puts the first responses of the two arms side by side: in one the action is in content, in the other it is in tool_calls.

deep-dive-under-the-hood.title.text: Native calling is text underneath too

deep-dive-under-the-hood.summary.text: What the model writes is still a string of tokens; the provider just parses it into fields by an agreed format.

deep-dive-under-the-hood.paragraphs.0.text: A model only generates tokens, and native tool calling is no exception. The provider first assembles messages and tools into one long text using the chat template the model was trained with, with special tokens separating the system prompt, user messages, tool definitions, and tool results. When the model proposes a call, what it writes is text with special tokens, and the provider parses it into the tool_calls field before returning. The chat templates of open models are public, so you can see this step directly; most commercial services don't publish the details. Unit 1 of the Hugging Face Agents Course shows what messages look like after they are assembled into template text.

deep-dive-under-the-hood.paragraphs.1.text: The model's way of producing output hasn't changed. Native calling is more reliable because of two things: the model has been trained specifically to end its turn after proposing a call, and the parsing is done by the provider in a fixed format. Some services also restrict the allowed tokens during generation so that the arguments fit a given structure. How exactly differs by provider; follow the provider's documentation. For the program, the result is a ready-made field, with no regular expression to write.

mq-native.native-saves.prompt.text: Compared with a text protocol, which step does native tool calling save the program?

mq-native.native-saves.a.text.text: Parsing the tool name and arguments out of free text

mq-native.native-saves.a.feedback.text: Correct. That step is handed to the provider.

mq-native.native-saves.b.feedback.text: Not quite. Execution is still the program's job.

mq-native.native-saves.c.text.text: Checking whether the arguments are valid

mq-native.native-saves.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The arguments can still be wrong, and the program still has to validate them.

mq-native.native-saves.explanation.text: Native calling changes how an action is represented; the responsibility for execution and validation doesn't change.

section-6.paragraphs.0.text: Use native tool calling when you can, and keep text protocols for places that lack that field. Every lesson after this one that needs tool calls uses native tool calling. Text protocols still have a place: the model or API doesn't support the tools parameter; you want the model to write a piece of code that can run directly rather than a JSON action; or you want to save the whole trace as plain text that people can read.

section-6.paragraphs.1.text: Code actions are another kind of text protocol. The Hugging Face Agents Course separates JSON agents from code agents by how the action is written, and counts function calling as a subtype of JSON agents. A code action has the model write a piece of Python for the program to execute. Loops, conditions, and multiple calls can all go into one piece of code, which is more flexible than JSON; the price is that you execute code the model wrote, so you need an isolation plan first. This platform's lessons currently don't execute model-generated code. Coding agents often take a middle road: Claude Code uses native tool calling, and its built-in `Bash` tool puts the command to run in a parameter. The model can chain several steps into one command, nearly as flexible as a code action, while the command sits in a structured field and doesn't have to be found in free text. The official tool list marks it as a tool that needs permission, and whether the user is asked before it runs depends on the permission settings (follow the official documentation).

section-6.paragraphs.2.text: Whichever protocol you use, three things stay the same: tool results must come from real execution; format errors must be recorded and not quietly fixed; and before you adopt the model's conclusion, confirm that what it saw was a real result. The next lesson, {{lesson:todo-planning}}, goes back to native tool calling and handles a multi-step task that looks things up three times and then saves a card.

misconception-no-stop.claim.text: The system prompt already says "Stop right after Action Input", so the model will comply and the request doesn't need stop.

misconception-no-stop.correction.text: A prompt is only a request. The model writes on by probability and may follow the demonstrated format into an Observation. stop is enforced by the provider: the model is cut off as soon as it writes that string, with no reliance on the model's self-discipline. Even with stop, the runner should check the output for a self-written observation, because the model might write it a different way to get around it.

code-parse.n62.text.text: The parser turns a piece of text the model wrote into one of three outcomes: an action, a final answer, or a parse failure.

code-parse.n68.text.text: First split at Observation:. What comes before is the part the model should write; what comes after is the part it shouldn't.

code-parse.n74.text.text: The conclusion after the model's self-written result is recorded separately, only to compare with the real result, and is never trusted.

code-parse.n78.text.text: Look for the action only in the part before the cut; an Action inside the self-written Observation doesn't count.

code-parse.n82.text.text: raw_decode reads only the one JSON value at the start, which is the parser's one leniency.

code-parse.n85.text.text: The arguments must be a JSON object; a string or array counts as a parse failure, and the parser doesn't rewrite it for the model.

code-parse.n91.text.text: With neither an action nor a Final Answer, it is judged a parse failure; nothing is guessed from the sentence.

code-text-loop.n105.text.text: t is the runtime text in this run's language: the system prompt, the question and the report text all come from it.

code-text-loop.n104.text.text: The step limit is the model-call budget; the text protocol needs one request at every step.

code-text-loop.n108.text.text: Only the arm with stop sends the stop parameter; that is the only difference between the two text arms.

code-text-loop.n113.text.text: Every output emits a lesson.parse, recording the original text, the parse result, and finish_reason together.

code-text-loop.n120.text.text: A parse failure stops the run at once, with no retry and no repair.

code-text-loop.n127.text.text: The runner calls the tool from the parse result: the tool_call and tool_result events from call_tool both carry origin: course_program, and the UI shows them as "Runner calls a tool".

code-text-loop.n131.text.text: The Observation the model wrote itself is recorded alongside the real result, for easy comparison.

code-text-loop.n136.text.text: Only the text before Observation and the real result are put back into the context.

code-text-loop.n139.text.text: Finally, check the final message history for any self-written Observation that slipped in; the result becomes the report's first check.

code-native.n146.text.text: The same question with native tool calling: the provider returns the action in structured form in the tool_calls field.

code-native.n152.text.text: The native arm puts the tool definition in tools, no longer requires the model to follow a text format, and doesn't need stop.

code-native.n155.text.text: The action is in the tool_calls field, so the program parses no text with a regex.

code-native.n158.text.text: With no proposed call, it ends and content is the final answer; in the text protocol this step depends on finding Final Answer.

code-native.n162.text.text: The assistant message with the proposed call is put back into the history first, so the later tool message has a call id to pair with.

code-native.n164.text.text: execute_proposal records the call and result by the id the model gave, the same way run_agent, the platform's native loop, executes.

code-native.n165.text.text: The tool result goes back in a message with role tool, instead of posing as an Observation from the user.

code-decision.title.text: Strict parsing: stop on failure, and don't fix the format for the model

code-decision.chosen.text: The parser accepts only two formats, Action / Action Input or Final Answer, and uses raw_decode to read the first JSON value of Action Input. Everything else is recorded as a lesson.parse with ok set to false, and the run stops. An Observation the model wrote itself is cut off and recorded separately, and doesn't enter the context.

code-decision.lenient-repair.title.text: Lenient repair: add quotes, add braces, dig arguments out of a sentence

code-decision.lenient-repair.why_not.text: When the repair succeeds you can't see that the model actually got it wrong; when it fails, what gets executed is arguments the program guessed, not the arguments the model proposed.

code-decision.retry-on-error.title.text: On a parse failure, send the error back to the model to rewrite

code-decision.retry-on-error.why_not.text: This is a workable approach, but it buries "unstable format" in the retry count. This lesson first keeps failures visible as they are; the approach of handing the error back to the model to rewrite was already shown in {{lesson:structured-output}}.

code-decision.trust-final-answer.title.text: Adopt the model's Final Answer as soon as it writes one

code-decision.trust-final-answer.why_not.text: Without stop, the Final Answer may rest on an Observation the model made up itself.

stop-vs-no-stop.guide.0.text.text: All three arms use the same text protocol; the only difference is whether the request carries stop. First look at the request.

stop-vs-no-stop.guide.1.text.text: With stop, the provider cuts the output off before the model writes "Observation:".

stop-vs-no-stop.guide.2.text.text: This is the original text of the model's first output. Without stop, see whether it keeps writing after Action Input.

stop-vs-no-stop.guide.3.text.text: When the runner sees that the model wrote an Observation itself, it cuts it out and records it as a separate event.

stop-vs-no-stop.guide.4.text.text: These are the real numbers from the score table. Compare them with what the model wrote above.

stop-vs-no-stop.guide.5.text.text: If the program took the Final Answer the model wrote as is, this is what the user would get.

stop-vs-no-stop.guide.6.text.text: In request 2, the part the model wrote itself has been removed, and the last message is the real result.

stop-vs-no-stop.guide.7.text.text: The final answer rests on the real result.

stop-vs-no-stop.conclusion.proves.0.text: In this run, whether the model wrote an Observation itself, what it wrote, and whether it agrees with the real tool result.

stop-vs-no-stop.conclusion.proves.1.text: The runner kept the self-written Observation out of later requests, and the final answer comes from the output after the model saw the real result.

stop-vs-no-stop.conclusion.does_not_prov.text: One run without fabrication doesn't mean this model never fabricates without stop; the reverse holds too.
stop can only cut at a string. If the model writes it another way (such as a lowercase "observation:"), stop doesn't catch it.
The fabricated content in offline test mode is written by a deterministic script and doesn't represent the behavior of any real model.

text-vs-native.title.text: Text protocol vs. native tool calling

text-vs-native.hypothesis.text: For the same question, the text protocol's action appears in content and the program has to parse it; native calling's action appears in the tool_calls field, the program parses no free text, and the tool result comes back in a tool message.

text-vs-native.text-content.text.text: The content of response 1: the text protocol's action is written here.

text-vs-native.native-calls.text.text: The tool_calls of response 1: native calling's action is written here.

text-vs-native.parse-event.text.text: The text protocol's parse result; the native arm has no such event.

text-vs-native.result-message.text.text: How the tool result comes back in request 2: in the text protocol it is Observation text; in native calling it is a message with role tool.

text-vs-native.guide.0.text.text: Both arms ask the same question. First see where in the response the model's action appears.

text-vs-native.guide.1.text.text: The text protocol's action is a piece of text in content.

text-vs-native.guide.2.text.text: Native calling's action is in the tool_calls field, where the tool name and arguments are separate fields.

text-vs-native.guide.3.text.text: Compare finish_reason: the text protocol is cut off by stop, and native calling ends with tool_calls.

text-vs-native.guide.4.text.text: Only the text protocol needs the program to parse; the native arm has no such step at run time.

text-vs-native.guide.5.text.text: The tool result also comes back differently: in one as plain text, in the other as a tool message with a tool_call_id.

text-vs-native.conclusion.proves.0.text: The two arms' actions appear in content and tool_calls respectively, and the parse event appears only in the text protocol arm.

text-vs-native.conclusion.proves.1.text: In both arms the tool is executed by the program; the message form that carries the result back differs.

text-vs-native.conclusion.does_not_prove.text: It doesn't show that native calling is always more accurate; it only hands the format problem to the provider, and the arguments can still be filled in wrong.
One tool and one question can't represent how the two protocols perform on multi-tool, multi-step tasks.

quiz.q1.prompt.text: A text-protocol request has stop: ["Observation:"]. What does it do?

quiz.q1.a.text.text: It makes the provider cut off the output before the model writes Observation:

quiz.q1.a.feedback.text: Correct. After the cut, control returns to the program, which executes the tool.

quiz.q1.b.text.text: It tells the model not to call tools

quiz.q1.b.feedback.text: Not quite. stop is just a stop string; it doesn't change whether the model can propose an action.

quiz.q1.c.text.text: It makes the provider execute the Action automatically

quiz.q1.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The provider doesn't know the Action format.

quiz.q1.explanation.text: stop leaves it to the provider to guarantee where the model's writing ends.

quiz.q2.prompt.text: The model's output contains an Observation and a Final Answer, but the program hasn't executed any tool yet. Can this Final Answer be used?

quiz.q2.a.text.text: No, because the observation it rests on was written by the model itself

quiz.q2.a.feedback.text: Correct. The tool was never executed, so the observation can't be real.

quiz.q2.b.text.text: Yes, because the model's format is exactly right

quiz.q2.b.feedback.text: Not quite. A correct format doesn't mean the content came from real execution.

quiz.q2.c.text.text: Yes, as long as the numbers look reasonable

quiz.q2.c.feedback.text: Not quite. "Looks reasonable" is exactly why made-up content is so hard to spot.

quiz.q2.explanation.text: To decide whether an answer is usable, look at where the evidence it rests on came from.

quiz.q5.prompt.text: Without stop, the model went on to write an Observation after Action Input. What is the most direct reason?

quiz.q5.a.text.text: The model continued along the demonstrated format and didn't know this line should wait for the program to write it

quiz.q5.a.feedback.text: Correct. The model is just writing the most likely next text; it has no way to actually look up the score table.

quiz.q5.b.feedback.text: Not quite. The model can only output text, and only the program can execute tools; this time the numbers were guessed.

quiz.q5.c.text.text: The provider inserted the tool result into the model's output

quiz.q5.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The provider doesn't know this text format and doesn't execute tools.

quiz.q5.explanation.text: Making the model stop relies on a provider-enforced mechanism such as stop, not on the model's self-discipline.

quiz.q3.prompt.text: The parser receives Action Input: {student_id: s-1042}. What is the right way to handle it?

quiz.q3.a.text.text: Record a parse failure with the original text and the reason, then stop

quiz.q3.a.feedback.text: Correct. A failure has to be visible before anyone can fix it.

quiz.q3.b.text.text: Add the quotes automatically and execute

quiz.q3.b.feedback.text: Not quite. Even if the fix is right, it hides the fact that the model's format is unstable; if it's wrong, the wrong arguments get executed.

quiz.q3.c.text.text: Treat it as no arguments and call the tool anyway

quiz.q3.c.feedback.text: Not quite. That amounts to executing a call the model never proposed.

quiz.q3.explanation.text: The parser's job is to convert faithfully, not to make decisions for the model.

quiz.q4.prompt.text: Why doesn't native tool calling have the problem of "the model writing the Observation itself"?

quiz.q4.a.text.text: A tool result can only be brought back by the program in a message with role tool

quiz.q4.a.feedback.text: Correct. The model's output has no place for a tool result.

quiz.q4.b.text.text: The model is smarter in native calling

quiz.q4.b.feedback.text: Not quite. The same model can use both protocols; the difference is in the protocol's structure.

quiz.q4.c.text.text: Native calling doesn't need to execute tools

quiz.q4.c.feedback.text: Not quite. Tools are still executed by the program.

quiz.q4.explanation.text: The structure of the protocol decides which content can only be supplied by the program.

check-hunt.prompt.text: Run "Text protocol, without stop" and find the step where the runner discovers that the model wrote an Observation itself.

check-hunt.explanation.text: This event puts together the Observation the model wrote itself, the real tool result, and the Final Answer the model wrote itself. At this step the runner cut off the self-written part, and later requests contain only the real result. If your run has no such event, this run didn't reach the cut-and-record step: the model may have stopped right after Action Input, or its output may have failed to parse. Compare against the original text in lesson.parse to tell which; you can run again or compare with another model.

check-points.prompt.text: Compare against your own run and this lesson's source, and tick each item once you've done it.

check-points.item-1.text.text: I compared the original text of the first output in the run with stop and the run without stop.

check-points.item-2.text.text: I can point out which two events hold the Observation the model wrote itself and the real tool result.

check-points.item-3.text.text: I can say which step native tool calling saves and which responsibilities it keeps.

code_notes.stop.note.text: A request parameter whose value is a list of stop sequences. In this lesson it is ["Observation:"], sent only by the "With stop" arm.

code_notes.finish_reason.note.text: States in the response why the output ended: stop means it ended naturally or hit a stop sequence, and tool_calls means a tool call was proposed.

code_notes.tool_calls.note.text: A structured field in the assistant message: each call has an id, a tool name, and arguments as a JSON string.

code_notes.lesson.parse.note.text: The parse record for each model output: original text, result type (action / final answer / failure), ok, error.

code_notes.lesson.fabricated_observation.text: Emitted when the model writes an Observation itself: shows side by side what it made up, the real tool result, and the Final Answer it wrote from that.

code_notes.raw_decode.note.text: A Python standard-library method: parses only the one JSON value at the start of a string and doesn't raise an error for extra text after it.
